title: Tiresias
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: With Bacchus safe in his cradle, the poem turns to a quarrel in heaven: Jupiter, loosened by nectar, tells Juno that women get more pleasure out of love than men do, and she denies it. They send for Tiresias, who is qualified because he has known love from both sides — seven autumns as a woman after striking a pair of coupling snakes with his staff, and then back again when he struck the same pair a second time — and he decides for Jupiter; Juno blinds him for it, and since no god may undo what another god has done, Jupiter pays for the lost eyes with knowledge of the future. Watch the legal vocabulary — arbiter, suit, sentence — running straight through a bedroom joke; the mismatch is the joke.

sentences.t:
Dumque ea per terras fatali lege geruntur
tutaque bis geniti sunt incunabula Bacchi,
sentences.l: And while these things are being carried on over the earth by the law of fate, and the cradle of twice-born Bacchus is safe,
sentences.i: And while all this was going forward on earth under fate's law, and the cradle of twice-born Bacchus was safe,
sentences.n: Dum with a present indicative describes something going on in past time — English needs "was." Incunabula, a plural noun for swaddling-bands and so for a cradle, picks the story up exactly where the last one set it down; and bis genitus, "twice-born," is the epithet the previous tale has just earned him — womb first, then thigh.

sentences.t:
forte Iovem memorant, diffusum nectare, curas
seposuisse graves vacuumque agitasse remissos
cum Iunone iocos
sentences.l: they relate that Jupiter, as it happened, mellowed with nectar, had laid aside his heavy cares and, being at leisure, had plied easy jokes with Juno,
sentences.i: the story goes that Jupiter, expansive with nectar, had set his heavy cares aside and, with nothing on his hands, was trading easy jokes with Juno,
sentences.n: Memorant, "they relate," governs a string of perfect infinitives (seposuisse, agitasse, dixisse): the whole scene is reported at second hand, which is Ovid holding it at arm's length from the start. Diffusum is "spread out, expanded" — what drink does to a man. Agitare iocos is to keep a joke going, to banter. Magnus prints vacuum, accusative masculine agreeing with Iovem, so Jupiter is the one with time on his hands; some editions print vacua, which puts the leisure on Juno's side of the scene instead.

sentences.t:
et “maior vestra profecto est,
quam quae contingit maribus” dixisse “voluptas.”
sentences.l: and to have said: "Your pleasure is assuredly greater than the pleasure that falls to males."
sentences.i: and to have said: "The pleasure you get is certainly greater than what falls to men."
sentences.n: Vestra is plural: Jupiter is not talking about Juno but about women as a class, which is part of why she takes it as she does. Voluptas is held back past the verb of speaking to the very last word of the sentence, so the Latin names the subject only when the sentence is over. Contingit is the ordinary word for what falls to one's lot. The pleasure at issue is pleasure in bed — voluptas needs no qualifier in Latin, and Ovid gives it none.

sentences.t:
Illa negat. Placuit quae sit sententia docti
quaerere Tiresiae:
sentences.l: She denies it. It was resolved to ask what the opinion of learned Tiresias might be:
sentences.i: She said no. It was resolved that they should ask learned Tiresias for his opinion:
sentences.n: Placuit is impersonal and formal, the verb of a body passing a resolution — it is what a senate does, and it makes the summoning a joint act rather than either god's. Quae sit is an indirect question, hence the subjunctive. Docti is dry: the learning that qualifies him here is of one very particular kind.

sentences.l: To him love-making of each kind was known.
sentences.i: He had known love from both sides.
sentences.n: Venus with a small letter is the act rather than the goddess — Latin uses the god's name for the thing she governs, which is why the literal says love-making and not "Venus." Utraque is "each of the two": he has had it as a man and as a woman, which is the whole reason the court sends for him.

sentences.t:
Nam duo magnorum viridi coeuntia silva
corpora serpentum baculi violaverat ictu;
sentences.l: For two bodies of great snakes, coupling in a green wood, he had violated with the blow of a staff;
sentences.i: For he had struck two great snakes as they coupled in a green wood, and done them violence with his staff;
sentences.n: Coeuntia is the ordinary verb for animals mating, "coming together." Violaverat means to profane as much as to injure — the blow is an offence, which is why it is answered. And look at the word order: duo ... corpora ... serpentum is prised apart and viridi ... silva laid inside it, so that the phrase itself is a tangle.

sentences.t:
deque viro factus (mirabile) femina septem
egerat autumnos.
sentences.l: and, from a man made (astonishing) a woman, he had passed seven autumns.
sentences.i: and, turned from a man into a woman — astonishing — he had lived out seven autumns so.
sentences.n: The grammar shows the seam: factus stays masculine while femina names the new sex, so the one participle holds both states at once. Mirabile is a one-word parenthesis, the poet stepping in to say he knows how this sounds. Agere autumnos is to pass years, counted by their season.

sentences.t:
Octavo rursus eosdem
vidit, et “est vestrae si tanta potentia plagae”
dixit “ut auctoris sortem in contraria mutet,
nunc quoque vos feriam.”
sentences.l: In the eighth he saw the same ones again, and said: "If there is such power in a blow struck on you that it turns the striker's condition into its opposite, now too I will strike you."
sentences.i: In the eighth he saw the same pair again, and said: "If a blow struck on you has power enough to turn the striker's condition into its opposite, then I'll strike you now as well."
sentences.n: Octavo has no noun with it: the autumnos of the line before supplies it, "in the eighth [autumn]." Si is postponed to third word and the phrase vestrae ... plagae is split around it and around tanta potentia, so the clause is under way two words before its own conjunction arrives — normal in verse, and worth reading twice. Vestrae plagae is the blow dealt to you, not by you — an objective genitive; and auctor is the one who deals it, that is, Tiresias himself, speaking of his own case in the third person like a man stating a legal principle. In contraria is neuter plural, "into the opposite state."

sentences.t:
Percussis anguibus isdem
forma prior rediit genetivaque venit imago.
sentences.l: The same snakes having been struck, his earlier form returned and the appearance he was born with came back.
sentences.i: With the same snakes struck, his former shape returned, and the body he was born in came back.
sentences.n: Percussis anguibus isdem is an ablative absolute — a self-contained "with X done" phrase where English wants a whole clause. Isdem is the edition's spelling of eisdem. Forma prior and genetiva imago say one thing twice in different words, the variation Ovid uses instead of repeating himself.

sentences.t:
Arbiter hic igitur sumptus de lite iocosa
dicta Iovis firmat.
sentences.l: He therefore, taken on as arbiter in the joking suit, confirms the words of Jove.
sentences.i: So he, appointed arbiter in the joking suit, upheld what Jove had said.
sentences.n: Arbiter, lis and firmat are all courtroom words: an arbiter is a privately agreed judge, a lis is a suit at law, and firmare is to uphold a contention. The comedy is the machinery, not the verdict — a marital argument about sex is being tried under civil procedure. Firmat is a historic present, dropping us into the scene.

sentences.t:
Gravius Saturnia iusto
nec pro materia fertur doluisse, suique
iudicis aeterna damnavit lumina nocte.
sentences.l: Saturnia is said to have grieved more heavily than was just, and not in proportion to the matter, and she condemned the eyes of her own judge to everlasting night.
sentences.i: Saturnia, they say, took it harder than was fair, and out of all proportion to what was at stake, and she sentenced her own judge's eyes to unending night.
sentences.n: Iusto is an ablative of comparison, "than what is just"; pro materia is "in proportion to the subject-matter," as of a penalty fitted to a case. Fertur with a perfect infinitive, "is said to have," is the second time in twenty lines that Ovid attributes the story to other people. Damnare with an ablative of the punishment is the formal sentencing idiom — so the legal language runs all the way through to the sentence, and sui iudicis makes the point: the judge she blinds is the judge in her own suit.

sentences.t:
At pater omnipotens (neque enim licet inrita cuiquam
facta dei fecisse deo) pro lumine adempto
scire futura dedit, poenamque levavit honore.
sentences.l: But the all-powerful father (for it is not permitted to any god to have made void the deeds done by a god) in exchange for the light taken away gave [him] to know things to come, and lightened the punishment with an honour.
sentences.i: But the almighty father — since no god is allowed to undo what a god has done — gave him, in return for the sight taken from him, knowledge of what was to come, and eased the punishment with an honour.
sentences.n: Inrita facere is to render null, to cancel; the rule that one god cannot annul another god's act is the hinge the whole scene turns on, and it is stated in a parenthesis. Licet takes a dative of the person permitted, and here the two halves of it are split — cuiquam ... deo, "to any god" — with the parenthesis and the line end lying between them. Inrita is the edition's spelling for irrita and is kept as it stands. Scire futura is an infinitive serving as the object of dedit, "gave [him] to know the future" — a Greek-flavoured construction, and dedit has no object of its own in the Latin, which is why the literal brackets one in. This is the prophetic gift that makes this Tiresias in every story after.
